title: Vesak, the fourth time
hook: Vesak as the schools keep it, side by side

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the block on practice traditions, and your line was choose one. Which practice did you pick up, and did you get to do it once, small? Day one thousand four hundred thirteen.

Four scenes, all in honor of one person. In a Sri Lankan town, a lit gateway the height of a house shows a story from the Buddha's past lives, and a stall hands out free drinks. In a Japanese temple courtyard, children ladle sweet tea over a tiny statue of a baby with one hand pointing up. In Seoul, a river of paper lotus lanterns moves through the streets at night. In Lhasa, pilgrims walk the circuit around the old city all month long, prayer wheels turning. Different dates, different food, different music. This is your fourth time meeting Vesak on this path. So today, instead of standing in one country, stand where you can see them all at once.
screen: `GATEWAYS AND FREE DRINKS.` → `SWEET TEA OVER A BABY.` → `LANTERNS AND A HOLY MONTH.`

segments.voice: Start with Vesak as Theravada lands keep it. There, like Sri Lanka, Thailand and Myanmar, one full moon remembers three things together: the Buddha's birth, his awakening and his passing away. That's your line today: born, awake, gone. Next, the schools that separate them. In Japan, the birth stands on its own, at the flower festival in spring, with the sweet tea and the pointing baby. The awakening has its own day in winter, and the passing its own day too. Korean and Chinese communities also keep the birthday as its own feast, with lanterns and the bathing of a small Buddha statue. Then Tibet. There, a whole month, Saga Dawa, is set apart. Its full moon remembers the awakening and the passing, and in some tellings the birth as well. Some Tibetan teachers say that good and harmful actions done in that month carry extra weight. Now set them side by side. The dates differ. The music differs. But underneath, the same thing is being said. The Dhammapada has a short verse for it, in Max Müller's words: "Happy is the arising of the awakened." Each school, in its own way, is glad that this person was born, woke up, and taught. And here's the quiet part. A festival kept side by side isn't a contest over who keeps it best. A lantern in Seoul and a lamp in Colombo are both lit for the same arrival.
screen: `ONE MOON, THREE EVENTS.` · `SEPARATE DAYS IN JAPAN.` · `A HOLY MONTH IN TIBET.` · then, large: `HAPPY IS THE ARISING.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or a small lamp, you can light it now, safely, somewhere you can see it. If not, a phone screen turned low, or just the light in the window, will do. Sit facing it. Let the breath settle. With the first few breaths, think: born. A small life arriving. With the next few: awake. Eyes open, seeing clearly. With the next: gone. A flame that will, one day, go out. Then let the words fall away and just watch the light. Stay with it for the rest of the time. The bell holds the time.
Vesak. The full moon on which Theravada Buddhists remember the birth, the awakening and the passing, kept in different ways by different schools. Today's word.
Your line: born, awake, gone. Today, when you turn on a light, say the three words once to yourself. Day one thousand four hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: In Theravada countries, Buddhists keep Vesak on a full moon with temple visits, extra precepts, giving and lamps; in Japan, Korea and China the birth is often kept as its own day, and in Tibet the month of Saga Dawa is set apart.
